steps.body: The best way to know a shape's rules is to meet the shapes that ALMOST pass. A 'misfit' breaks exactly one rule — and that one break shows you which rule was doing the work. Non-examples teach the definition from the outside in.
Use the closed-shape rule to test a near-miss.

widget.prompt: An open figure made from three straight segments is a triangle. Is this always, sometimes, or never true?
widget.blocker: A triangle must be closed, but the open figure has a gap.

choices.label: Never
choices.feedback: Yes. The gap breaks the closed-shape rule every time.
choices.evidenceText: A triangle must be closed; this figure is open.

choices.label: Sometimes
choices.feedback: As long as the gap remains, the figure cannot be a triangle. There is no valid example.
choices.evidenceText: The open corner blocks triangle membership.

choices.label: Always
choices.feedback: Three segments are not enough. A triangle's sides must join to make a closed figure.
choices.evidenceText: The gap breaks the triangle definition.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Check the whole definition: three straight sides and a fully closed shape.
widget.successFeedback: Never. The open corner is a blocker, so the figure is not a triangle until the gap closes.

predict.prompt: An open figure made from three straight segments is a triangle. Is this always, sometimes, or never true?

options.label: Never
Sometimes
Always

predict.reveal: A triangle must be closed. The gap blocks the definition every time, even when the figure has three straight segments.

explanationVariants: A curved side breaks the 'all sides straight' rule — the count and closure are fine, but a triangle's sides must be straight.
Everything else checks out; the curve alone disqualifies it, pointing straight at the straightness rule.

widget.prompt: A closed figure has three sides, but one side is curved like a bow. Which rule does it break?

options.label: 'All sides must be straight'
options.feedback: Three sides ✓, closed ✓ — only the curve fails. That's the straightness rule at work.

options.label: 'Must have exactly three sides'
options.feedback: It DOES have three sides — the count is fine. The problem is the curved one, which breaks 'straight sides.'

options.label: 'Must be closed'
options.feedback: It's closed all the way around — no gap. The rule it breaks is straightness, because of the curved side.

options.label: It breaks no rule — it's a triangle
options.feedback: A curved side means it can't be a triangle. Triangles need three STRAIGHT sides — that's the broken rule.

steps.body: Misfits are sneaky because they look close. A four-sided figure with three lovely square corners feels rectangle-ish — until you check the fourth corner and find it tilted. **A rectangle needs ALL four corners square; break even one, and it drops out of the club.** One flaw is enough.

explanationVariants: A rectangle requires all four corners square; three-out-of-four fails the rule, so it's not a rectangle.
Close isn't enough — the one tilted corner breaks the 'four right angles' rule completely.

widget.prompt: A four-sided shape has three square corners and one tilted corner. Is it a rectangle?

options.label: No — a rectangle needs ALL four corners square
options.feedback: One tilted corner breaks the four-right-angles rule. Almost isn't in — the club checks every corner.

options.label: Yes — three square corners is close enough
options.feedback: The rule has no 'close enough.' All FOUR corners must be square; one tilted corner disqualifies it.

options.label: Yes — any four-sided shape is a rectangle
options.feedback: Four sides only makes a quadrilateral. A rectangle additionally needs four square corners — this shape is one short.

options.label: Only if the tilted corner is small
options.feedback: A corner is either square or it isn't — size of the tilt doesn't matter. One non-square corner breaks the rule.

widget.prompt: Rule: 'a square' (4 straight sides, 4 right angles, all sides equal). Sort each figure.

items.label: 4 equal straight sides, 4 square corners
items.feedback: Every rule met — a real square.

items.label: 4 equal sides, corners tilted
items.feedback: Equal sides but no right angles — that's a rhombus, a square-misfit (breaks the right-angle rule).

items.label: 4 square corners, sides 5 and 2
items.feedback: Square corners but unequal sides — a rectangle, a square-misfit (breaks the equal-sides rule).

items.label: 4 equal sides but one side curved
items.feedback: A curved side breaks 'straight sides' — misfit.

widget.missFeedback: A real square must pass ALL three extra rules; breaking any one makes it a misfit.
widget.successFeedback: Only the all-rules figure is a true square; the rhombus, rectangle, and curved one each break exactly one rule.

explanationVariants: A near-miss that breaks exactly one rule spotlights that rule — you learn what 'triangle' means by seeing what disqualifies a non-triangle.
Non-examples define the edges: the rule you didn't notice becomes obvious the moment a misfit breaks it.

widget.prompt: Why are 'almost' shapes (misfits) useful for learning a definition?

options.label: Each one breaks a single rule, showing exactly what that rule requires
options.feedback: A misfit spotlights the one rule it fails — the definition's edges become visible.

options.label: They prove the definition is wrong
options.feedback: Misfits don't break the definition — they CONFIRM it by showing what falls outside. The rules hold.

options.label: They're just tricky and teach nothing
options.feedback: The near-misses are the most instructive cases — each pinpoints a rule you might otherwise overlook.

options.label: They mean the shape has no rules
options.feedback: The opposite — a misfit exists precisely because it violates a rule. That violation teaches the rule.

hints: Check the square's three rules one at a time: straight sides, right angles, equal sides.
This figure has four straight sides and four square corners — so which rule is left to test?
explanationVariants: The figure passes 'straight sides' and 'four right angles,' so only 'all sides equal' is left — and with sides 7 and 4, it fails exactly that. It's a rectangle, rejected from the square club on the equal-sides rule.
Two rules pass, one fails: unequal sides (7 ≠ 4) breaks the equal-sides rule, making it a rectangle, not a square.

widget.prompt: A detective rejects a figure from the SQUARE club. It has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners, but its sides are 7 and 4. Which rule got it rejected?

options.label: 'All sides equal' — its sides are 7 and 4
options.feedback: Straight ✓, right angles ✓, but 7 ≠ 4 breaks equal-sides. It's a rectangle, not a square.

options.label: 'Four right angles' — corners failed
options.feedback: The corners ARE square (given). The rule it fails is equal-sides: 7 and 4 aren't equal.

options.label: 'Straight sides' — a side is curved
options.feedback: All four sides are straight (given). The disqualifier is the unequal side lengths, 7 and 4.

options.label: It shouldn't have been rejected — it's a square
options.feedback: A square needs equal sides, and 7 ≠ 4. It's a rectangle — correctly rejected from the square club.

takeaways: A misfit breaks exactly one rule — and that break reveals the rule.
'Almost' never counts: one broken rule drops a shape from the club.
Non-examples define a shape as sharply as examples do.
steps.teaser: next chapter: splitting shapes into fair, equal parts — geometry shakes hands with fractions.

concept.body: Quick rewind. A misfit is a shape that **fails the entry test on exactly one rule.** To find which rule, run down the checklist: right side-count? all straight? closed? all corners/sides as required? The first 'no' you hit is the broken rule.

explanationVariants: Four sides breaks the triangle's 'exactly 3 sides' rule.
A triangle needs three sides; four breaks the count rule.

widget.prompt: A closed figure with four straight sides is NOT a triangle. Which rule does it break?

options.label: 'Exactly 3 sides'
options.feedback: Four sides breaks the count — it's a quadrilateral, not a triangle.

options.label: 'Must be closed'
options.feedback: It IS closed. The broken rule is the side count: a triangle needs exactly three.

options.label: 'Straight sides'
options.feedback: All four sides are straight. What fails is the count — three sides required, not four.
